"Prior" means coming before something else — in time, in order, or in importance. It's a formal, precise way of saying "earlier" or "before."

The most important thing to grasp: "prior" is almost always relational. It doesn't describe a thing in isolation — it places one thing ahead of another, on a timeline or a ranking.
The Main Meaning: Earlier in Time or Order

This is how "prior" is used most of the time. Something "prior" happened, existed, or was arranged before something else.

  • "You need prior experience for this job."
    → Experience you had before you applied.
  • "He had no prior knowledge of the topic."
    → Before this moment, he knew nothing about it.
  • "She gave prior notice before quitting."
    → She informed them beforehand, not at the last minute.
  • "He had two prior convictions."
    → He had been convicted of crimes before this current case.

Notice that "prior" quietly tells you: this thing already existed or happened before the thing you are currently focused on. It establishes a before, relative to a now or a later.
A Deeper Layer: Prior Often Implies Relevance

"Prior" doesn't just mean earlier in a neutral sense. It usually carries the suggestion that the earlier thing matters to the present situation — it has a bearing, a claim, or a consequence on what's happening now.

Compare:

  • "I had a conversation with him yesterday." — neutral, just factual
  • "I had a prior conversation with him about this." — implies that conversation is relevant to what's being discussed now; it casts a shadow on the present

This is why "prior" appears so often in legal and professional language. In law, "prior convictions," "prior consent," and "prior claims" all describe earlier facts that directly affect the current situation. The earliness is the point — because it came first, it has standing.
A Secondary Sense: Higher in Importance or Precedence

Sometimes "prior" means not just "earlier," but "ranking above," "taking precedence," or "coming first in importance."

  • "She has a prior claim to the property."
    → Her claim must be addressed before all others; it outranks them.
  • "Family is a prior concern for him."
    → Among all his concerns, family ranks first.

This is where words like "priority" and "prioritize" come from. Something with priority is "prior" — it comes first, either in time or in rank.

In practice, these two senses overlap: a claim that was made earlier in time often also has precedence as a result. So "prior" can carry both ideas at once.

You'll very often see "prior to" used together as a phrase meaning before.

  • "Prior to the meeting, please read the report." → Before the meeting.
  • "She lived in Paris prior to moving to London." → Before she moved.
  • "No experience is required prior to joining." → Before joining.

"Prior to" is simply a formal, written version of "before." In casual speech, people say "before." In formal writing, official documents, legal language, and professional communication, "prior to" is the preferred form.

Prior vs. Previous

This is the most important distinction.

  • "Previous" is neutral. It just means the one that came before, without any particular implication. "My previous job." "The previous chapter." "A previous attempt." It could mean the one immediately before, or simply any one that came before.
  • "Prior" is more weighted. It suggests that the earlier thing is relevant, official, or has a claim on the current situation. "Prior commitments" doesn't just mean earlier commitments — it means commitments that were made first and therefore must be honoured first. They have precedence. You'd never say "prior chapter" — because an earlier chapter doesn't carry legal or relational weight over a later one; "previous chapter" would be the right choice.
  • "Prior" is also more formal than "previous."

Prior vs. Former

  • "Former" means "was, but is no longer." "My former boss" = someone who used to be my boss but isn't anymore. "The former president" = no longer in office.
  • "Prior" carries no such "no longer" sense. It simply means before. "Prior experience" doesn't imply that experience is gone; it just means experience from before.

Prior vs. Earlier

  • "Earlier" is the most everyday, casual word for things that came before in time. "I saw him earlier." "Call me earlier next time."
  • "Prior" is more formal and implies a meaningful, often official, connection to the present. You'd write "no prior authorization required" in a formal document, not "no earlier authorization required" — it would sound off.

"Prior" is a formal word. It lives most comfortably in:

  • Legal contexts: prior offense, prior consent, prior art (existing inventions before a patent application), prior restraint
  • Workplace and professional settings: prior approval, prior experience, prior notice, prior authorization
  • Academic writing: prior research, prior studies, prior literature

In everyday spoken conversation, people rarely say "prior." They naturally say "before," "earlier," or "previous." If you hear or read "prior," there's usually a formal or official tone to the context.
Common Pairings (Words That Naturally Go with "Prior")

These are the combinations where "prior" is most naturally used. Getting familiar with them will help you recognize and use the word correctly:

  • prior experience — experience you already had before something begins
  • prior knowledge — knowledge you already possessed
  • prior notice — warning or information given beforehand
  • prior approval / authorization — getting permission before acting
  • prior commitment — an obligation already made before a new request arrives
  • prior conviction / offense — a crime committed before the current legal matter
  • prior consent — agreement obtained before the act
  • prior to — before (used as a preposition)
A Simple Way to Remember It

Think of "prior" as placing something in front — either on a timeline (it happened first) or on a list of importance (it ranks first).

Whenever you see "prior," ask yourself: before what? or ahead of what? The answer is usually clear from the sentence around it.

And whenever you feel the urge to write "before" in a formal, professional, or legal sentence, "prior to" is often the more appropriate and precise choice.
